Buying well

How to compare solar quotes without being fooled

Quotes are not comparable by default — different specs, different warranties, different fine print. How to normalise them into a table that tells the truth.

Published 10 June 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Three solar quotes arrive: $6,200, $7,900 and $5,400. The instinct is to compare the numbers. The correct move is to compare what each number buys — because quote prices only look comparable when the specifications behind them are, and they almost never are on first read.

Build one table, fill it three times

Take a sheet of paper or a spreadsheet and make these rows, one column per quote: system size and panel count; panel model and wattage; inverter model and type (plain string, optimised, hybrid); mounting system; isolation and protection components; monitoring hardware and platform; battery model if included, with usable kWh and kW; workmanship warranty length; product warranty lengths; expected annual generation and its stated assumption; installed price; incentive treatment and conditions; expected completion timing; payment schedule.

Where a quote cannot fill a row, leave it blank — the gaps are the comparison's most useful output. A quote that answers eight of fourteen rows is not a quote yet; it is a price.

Where the real differences hide

  • Inverter type — a hybrid inverter costs more than a plain string inverter and changes what a future battery requires. Two quotes at similar prices can differ by an entire upgrade path.
  • Panel performance curve — same warranty length, different guaranteed output and degradation allowances. The numbers in the performance warranty are where panel quality actually shows.
  • Mounting and protection components — isolators, cable, protection devices and roof sealing are where cheap quotes economise invisibly. Ask for brands, not just 'compliant'.
  • Monitoring — included or not, hardware or app-only, and who owns the data and the account.
  • Labour scope — switchboard work, cable runs, access equipment, cleanup and removal of packaging are all quotable line items that some quotes omit and then recover later as variations.
  • Battery specifics — usable capacity, continuous and peak power, and warranted throughput: the three numbers that decide what storage actually does.

Price red flags, in context

  • A price dramatically below every other quote for a like-for-like specification — something is being economised, delayed or conditional.
  • A discount that depends on beating a program deadline the seller cannot control.
  • A savings figure quoted to the dollar without stated rates and usage assumptions.
  • Pressure to decide on the first visit: genuine offers survive a night's sleep, and reputable sellers plan for one.

A worked comparison shape

The pattern that usually emerges: the middle quote carries the hybrid inverter and the named monitor; the cheapest has neither and a shorter workmanship warranty; the most expensive adds marginal panel efficiency that a larger array would have delivered for less. The right answer is rarely the cheapest or the dearest — it is the quote whose specification fits the household's five-year plan, at a price whose components can all be named.

Refusal to specify is information

If a seller will not put model numbers, warranty layers and assumptions in writing before you commit, that reluctance is itself a data point — and it belongs in the comparison table alongside the prices.

Key takeaways

  • Quotes are not comparable until normalised into the same specification rows.
  • Inverter type, panel performance curves, protection components and labour scope are the usual hidden differences.
  • Blank rows matter: a quote missing key specifications is a price, not an offer.
  • The best quote fits your plan; it is rarely the lowest or the highest.
  • Red flags cluster around urgency, unstated assumptions and vague discounts.
